tests.description: URI with leading-zero IPv4 is structurally valid as a reg-name
tests.comment: RFC 3986, Section 3.2.2: If an IP literal fails strict IPv4address parsing, it falls back to reg-name. A string of digits and dots is valid under unreserved characters. JSON Schema format asserts syntax, not scheme-specific DNS semantics.

tests.description: URI with out-of-bounds IPv4 is structurally valid as a reg-name
tests.comment: RFC 3986, Section 3.2.2: Fallback to reg-name allows digits and dots.
RFC 3986, Section 4.2: relative-part includes path-empty, which is zero characters.
RFC 3986, Section 4.2: relative-ref = relative-part [ "?" query ] [ "#" fragment ], so a query with an empty path is a reference.

tests.description: a network-path reference with an empty authority
tests.comment: RFC 3986, Section 3.2.2: host = IP-literal / IPv4address / reg-name, and reg-name may be empty.
RFC 3986, Section 3.2.2: square brackets are reserved for an IP-literal inside the authority. path-absolute is built from pchar, which excludes them.

tests.description: a leading zero in the IPv4 part of an IPv6 literal
tests.comment: RFC 3986, Section 3.2.2: inside an IP-literal the dotted quad must be an IPv4address, and dec-octet has no leading-zero alternative. There is no reg-name fallback inside brackets.

tests.description: a colon in the first segment preceded by a dot-segment
tests.comment: RFC 3986, Section 4.2: "Such a segment must be preceded by a dot-segment (e.g., \"./this:that\") to make a relative-path reference."
